title: “Funk”: Prelude and Fugue No.7, Book II
content_blocks: Prelude and Fugue No.7 from Book II is one of the lighter, more fun ones.  All of the pairs in Book II have subtitles; this one is subtitled “Funk,” since the piano preparations evoke a jazz quartet playing funk grooves.  The bass notes are prepared with wads of poster putty on some of the piano bass strings.  Stopping the strings at particular spots will produce a higher pitch (a ‘harmonic’).  But the added mass of the putty and the pencil will also lower the pitch of the original strings.  The conflict between two different sounding notes can create vibrato or even a glissando into notes—exactly like a jazz bassist!

Other bass strings have sponges placed between the strings, resulting in a low, pitchless sound similar to tom-tom drums.  Some of the higher strings are more aggressively dampened, sounding like jazz rim shots (where the butt-end of the drum stick rests on the head, while the shaft strikes the rim of the drum).  A few more modifications and I’ve got a drum set!  The tom-toms provide fills to the bass groove.  Other higher strings are stopped with poster putty only at the far end of the strings, with progressively less poster putty as the notes get lower.  This produces a xylophone- or marimba-like sound, which gradually turns into ordinary (unprepared) piano.  Bass, drums, xylophone, and piano—I’ve got a jazz quartet.

The prelude progresses in fairly-ordinary 8-bar phrases, with a 16-bar drum-set “break” in the middle.  But there is something curious:  the third beat of the measure is elongated by a sixteenth, as if everybody in the quartet agreed to just relax there for a bit…until the drum-set break, which exploits the strange meter to interesting effect.

Different harmonics on different strings can produce the same pitch.  The fugue takes advantage of this—along with detuning some of the strings with poster putty—to create a subject that is more rhythm and timbre than melody.  This subject is answered by the drum sounds, which are the perfect medium for a rhythmic and timbral fugue subject, before it progresses down through xylophone to piano.  The reduction in the importance of pitch leads to prolonged repetition of a single note in the piano, accompanied by a Dizzy Gillespie “Salt Peanuts” quote, which appears again at the end of the fugue.

The fugue is odd in two other ways. First, although there are never more than two voices sounding at once—so it’s a two-voice fugue—the subject does progress through all four instrumental groups, so it seems like a four-voice fugue. Second, where the third beat of the prelude is a sixteenth-note too long, in the fugue the third beat is a sixteenth-note too short. In effect, the prelude borrows that third-beat sixteenth-note from the fugue!

These pieces were inspired by some of the jazz of the 1960s and 1970s (Weather Report, Chick Corea and Return to Forever... also João Gilberto and Stan Getz)—music that grooves. They are also inspired by photographs of New York in the 1940s and 1950s, by such photographers as Todd Webb and Art Kane—see here and here.

You can listen to Michael Mizrahi’s exciting performances of the Prelude and the Fugue on YouTube, and you can watch a video of him recording the Prelude here. Fun facts about the video: in addition to the sponges in the bass strings, you can see that somebody was sitting at the right edge of the keyboard (yes, it was me), turning the pages for Michael and also making sure that the tambourine/jingle I had jury-rigged in the strings wouldn’t vibrate when they weren’t playing (I’ve got some ideas for a 3D printed version of the tambourine/jingle — if you know your way around 3D printing drop me a line). You can also see Michael break out into a smile at several points in the piece: he had been practicing on a regular (unprepared) piano, and it wasn’t until he got into the recording studio that he first heard what the piece actually sounded like. He dug the funk groove so much he smiled through much of the recording session.
